# True or false: People

Code assistants, hiring, onboarding, careers and sustainable pace. These statements test beliefs about how engineers join, grow and stay.

10 statements (Foundation 4, Standard 6). Decide whether each one is true or false before you open the answer. Every answer says why and links to the page that teaches it.

Prefer the terminal? From the repository root, run `python3 exercises/quiz.py --area people`.

### 1. If a code assistant wrote a line, the engineer who submitted it is not responsible for that line.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** The engineer who opens a change owns every line of it, however it was produced. They must be able to explain, test and support it. 'The assistant wrote it' is not an answer in review or in a postmortem.

Read more: [playbook/people/code-assistants.md](../../playbook/people/code-assistants.md)

</details>

### 2. Code written with an assistant should face the same review standard and size limits as any other change.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** The review bar does not change because a tool wrote the first draft. Same tests, same reviewers, same size limits and same security checks. Large generated pull requests waved through are a common failure.

Read more: [playbook/people/code-assistants.md](../../playbook/people/code-assistants.md)

</details>

### 3. The share of code generated by assistants is a good measure of their success.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** More generated code does not mean better outcomes; it can mean more to review and more to fix. Watch the DORA metrics, review load and developer surveys. If change fail rate or rework rate rises after adoption, act before expanding use.

Read more: [playbook/people/code-assistants.md](../../playbook/people/code-assistants.md)

</details>

### 4. Unstructured, conversational interviews predict job performance better than structured ones.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Research on selection methods (Schmidt and Hunter, 1998; Sackett and colleagues, 2022) finds the opposite. Structured interviews and work samples predict job performance better than unstructured conversations. Ask every candidate the same questions and score against a written scorecard.

Read more: [playbook/people/hiring.md](../../playbook/people/hiring.md)

</details>

### 5. Interviewers should discuss a candidate as a group before writing down their scores.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Once people hear the most senior or most confident voice, their own judgement shifts towards it. Each interviewer completes the scorecard independently first. The debrief then compares written evidence.

Read more: [playbook/people/hiring.md](../../playbook/people/hiring.md)

</details>

### 6. A new engineer should merge a first pull request within their first week.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** The playbook targets 5 working days or less, and 3 for a startup. That needs accounts ready and a working build on day one. A small, real first task chosen in advance makes it possible.

Read more: [playbook/people/onboarding.md](../../playbook/people/onboarding.md)

</details>

### 7. Moving into management should be the only route to senior pay for engineers.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A single route turns good senior engineers into reluctant managers, or sends them elsewhere. Publish parallel individual contributor and manager tracks with equal pay bands up to senior levels. Define levels by scope of impact.

Read more: [playbook/people/career-framework.md](../../playbook/people/career-framework.md)

</details>

### 8. Certifications such as CKA are the best measure of an engineer's skill.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Certifications give a structured syllabus and a signal, not proof of skill. Judge skill by the work people do. Pair any course with real work in the following weeks so it sticks.

Read more: [playbook/people/skills-gap.md](../../playbook/people/skills-gap.md)

</details>

### 9. Regular overtime is a sign that planning failed, not a sign of a committed team.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Tired engineers make more mistakes, and those mistakes reach production. Plan to about 80% of capacity and cut scope before adding hours. When a crunch does happen, give the time back.

Read more: [playbook/people/sustainable-pace.md](../../playbook/people/sustainable-pace.md)

</details>

### 10. Every critical system should have at least two people who can support it unaided.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** With one expert, a resignation or a holiday becomes an outage risk. Aim for a bus factor of 2 or more, built through pairing and rotations. Record the risk with an owner and a date wherever the bus factor is below 2.

Read more: [playbook/people/skills-gap.md](../../playbook/people/skills-gap.md)

</details>
